extraction.name: PIQA
extraction.description: A benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning framed as multiple-choice question answering over goal and solution pairs.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk; Rowan Zellers; Ronan Le Bras; Jianfeng Gao; Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected by prompting annotators with links to instructables.com and asking them to construct goal-solution pairs plus an invalid permutation, followed by validation from other annotators and removal of low-agreement examples.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: How-to instructions from instructables.com were used as prompts and inspiration for annotation.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset was cleaned using AFLite to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples, and examples with low agreement were removed during validation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were shown instructables for inspiration and asked to provide a physical goal, a valid solution, and a trick solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong; additional qualification and validation HITs were used.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low agreement were removed during validation, and human performance was calculated by majority vote.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors aim for PIQA to support progress toward language representations useful beyond NLP, including robotic-language applications.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses reporting bias in physical commonsense text and annotation artifacts, and describes prompting with instructables and AFLite filtering to reduce these biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Some examples require expert-level domain knowledge and were removed; some development errors judged as mistakes were actually correct but required web search to verify; the authors argue learning about the world from language alone is limiting.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating physical commonsense understanding in natural language models, including training, development, and testing splits.

name.evidence: In this paper, we introduce the task of physical commonsense reasoning and a corresponding benchmark dataset Physical Interaction: Question Answering or PIQA.

description.evidence: We introduce a new dataset, PIQA, for benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding. The underlying task is multiple choice question answering: given a question q and two possible solutions s1;s2, a model or a human must choose the most appropriate solution, of which exactly one is correct.

isLiveDataset.evidence: In total our dataset is comprised of over 16,000 training QA pairs with an additional ∼2K and ∼3k held out for development and testing, respectively.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: Specifically, annotators were asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable and pull out or have it inspire them to construct two component tasks. They would then articulate the goal (often centered on atypical materials) and how to achieve it. In addition, we asked them to provide a permutation to their own solution which makes it invalid, often subtly (Figure 3). Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Specifically, annotators were asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable and pull out or have it inspire them to construct two component tasks.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: Our dataset is inspired by instructables.com, which provides users with instructions on how to build, craft, bake, or manipulate objects using everyday materials. To achieve this, we provide a prompt to the annotators derived from instructables.com.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: The dataset is further cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm introduced in (Sakaguchi et al. 2020; Sap et al. 2019) which is an improvement on adversarial filtering (Zellers et al. 2018; Zellers et al. 2019b). During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: In the HIT design the instructable provides inspiration to think out-of-the-box (1 Sock, 3 Products) and annotators are asked for 1. a physical goal, 2. a valid solution, and 3. a trick. The trick should sound reasonable, but be wrong often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. Additional HITs (not shown) were run for qualification prior to this stage and validation afterwards.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. Human performance was calculated by a majority vote.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Key to our research aims in this work is helping to build language tools which capture enough physical knowledge to speed up the bootstrapping of robotic-language applications. Our goal with PIQA is to provide insight and a benchmark for progress towards language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced, to enable the construction of language models useful beyond the NLP community.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: We initially experimented with asking annotators for (task, tool) pairs via unconstrained prompts, but found that reporting bias swamped the dataset. As noted previously, we use AFLite (Sakaguchi et al. 2020) to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples from the data, which have been shown to artificially inflate model performance on previous NLI benchmarks.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g. special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of “commonsense.” Manual inspection of the development errors show that some “mistakes” are actually correct but required a web-search to verify. We have evaluated against large-scale pretrained models as they are in vogue as the de facto standard of progress within NLP, but are primarily interested in their performance and failings as a mechanism for advancing the position that learning about the world from language alone, is limiting.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We introduce a new dataset, PIQA, for benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding. In total our dataset is comprised of over 16,000 training QA pairs with an additional ∼2K and ∼3k held out for development and testing, respectively.
